issues.legal_issue: A will must be proved by its propounder, including removal of suspicious circumstances and proof of testamentary capacity and signature, even when secondary evidence is required because attesting witnesses cannot testify.
material_facts: A beneficiary relied on a will to exclude several properties from division in a family property dispute.
One attesting witness and the scribe had died before the evidence was taken; the other attesting witness was alive but unable to speak or move.
The beneficiary did not produce evidence establishing that the deceased attesting witness had attested the will, and the identifying witness did not testify to witnessing its execution.
There was no evidence establishing the testator’s mental and physical condition when the will was allegedly executed; evidence showed advanced age and serious physical and mental difficulties.
The courts found substantial differences among the testator’s signatures on the will, and the suspicious circumstances were not satisfactorily explained.
issues.conclusion: The will was not proved and could not establish that the properties it described were unavailable for division.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 68 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, a will required by law to be attested cannot be used in evidence unless an attesting witness is called, if one is alive, subject to process, and capable of giving evidence. The propounder bears the burden of proving due execution, the testator’s signature and testamentary capacity, and of dispelling suspicious circumstances. If primary evidence through an attesting witness cannot be given, secondary evidence may be led, as recognized in Daulat Ram v. Sodha, but the burden of proof remains. The approach to suspicious circumstances is consistent with Shashi Kumar Banerjee v. Subodh Kumar Banerjee and Pushpavathi v. Chandraraja Kadamba.

predicates.will_dispute: The proceeding concerns a property claim in which a beneficiary relies on a will to establish that property is not available for division.
predicates.attesting_witnesses_unavailable_or_incap: The attesting witnesses cannot provide testimony because they are dead or incapable of giving evidence.
predicates.secondary_evidence_does_not_establish_ex: The evidence offered in place of testimony from an attesting witness does not establish that the witness attested the document or that the testator executed it.
predicates.suspicious_circumstances_unresolved: Circumstances casting doubt on the testator’s signature, capacity, or freedom of choice remain unexplained.

issues.definition: When a will is relied on in a property dispute, the will is not proved if available witness testimony is absent, substitute evidence fails to establish execution, and suspicious circumstances remain unresolved.

issues.legal_issue: A party’s failure to file a replication does not by itself admit facts pleaded in a written statement when the opposing party has otherwise specifically challenged those facts.
material_facts: In a property division suit, a defendant pleaded in the written statement that the deceased had gifted certain properties to him.
The plaintiff did not file a replication but specifically denied the gift’s execution in affidavits concerning injunction applications.
Those affidavits were accepted on the record, and the parties proceeded to trial knowing that execution of the gift deed was disputed and led evidence on that issue.
issues.conclusion: The absence of a replication did not amount to an admission of the pleaded gift; the gift’s execution remained contested.
issues.legal_principle: Under Order VI Rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure, pleadings consist of the plaint and written statement; a replication, if permitted, may become part of the pleadings, but its absence does not itself admit facts pleaded in the written statement. Whether execution is specifically denied must be assessed in light of the record and the parties’ conduct. Rosammal Issetheenammal Fernandez v. Joosa Mariyan Fernandez holds that the existence of a specific denial determines whether the proviso to Section 68 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, applies.

predicates.civil_property_division_proceeding: The parties are litigating a claim to divide property and one party relies on a document pleaded in a written statement.
predicates.no_replication_filed: The opposing party did not file a replication responding to the written statement.
predicates.execution_specifically_denied_elsewhere_: The opposing party specifically challenged execution in another filing accepted by the court or otherwise made clear the challenge at trial.

issues.definition: In a property division proceeding, failure to file a replication does not admit an alleged document’s execution when execution has been specifically denied elsewhere in the record.

issues.legal_issue: A challenged gift deed must be proved when its execution is specifically denied, and failure to establish execution or the required attestation evidence prevents the deed from proving that the property was gifted.
material_facts: A beneficiary relied on a gift deed to exclude two properties from division.
The plaintiff challenged the validity and execution of the gift deed in filings and at trial, and the parties led evidence on that dispute.
One attesting witness had died, while the other was alive but was not examined; no reason was given for not examining the living witness.
The identifying witness denied signing as an identifying witness for the gift deed and said he did not know about the signature on it.
The evidence did not prove the document’s contents or the required handwriting and signatures; the gift deed was executed on the same day as a will that was also found suspicious and unproved.
issues.conclusion: The gift deed was not duly proved and could not establish that the properties had been gifted.
issues.legal_principle: Section 68 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, requires proof through an attesting witness where execution of a document required by law to be attested is specifically denied. The proviso dispensing with an attesting witness for a registered non-will document applies only if execution is not specifically denied. Where the attesting witnesses are not examined, Section 69 requires proof of the attestation and the executant’s signature in the manner stated by that provision. Rosammal Issetheenammal Fernandez v. Joosa Mariyan Fernandez explains the effect of specific denial under the proviso to Section 68.

rule.if: gift_deed_dispute and gift_execution_specifically_denied and attesting_witnesses_not_examined and required_signature_or_attestation_not_proved

predicates.gift_deed_dispute: The proceeding concerns property division and a party relies on a gift deed to claim property was transferred to that party.
predicates.gift_execution_specifically_denied: The opposing party specifically challenges execution of the gift deed in the record or at trial.
predicates.attesting_witnesses_not_examined: No attesting witness is called to testify about the gift deed.
predicates.required_signature_or_attestation_not_pr: The evidence does not establish the required attestation and the executant’s signature, or otherwise prove execution.

issues.definition: A gift deed relied on in a property division dispute is not proved when its execution is specifically denied, no attesting witness testifies, and the required signature or attestation is not established.

issues.legal_issue: The Supreme Court does not ordinarily disturb concurrent factual findings in a discretionary appeal when no basis for interference is shown.
material_facts: The trial court found the will and gift deed proved, but the first appellate court and the High Court found them unproved and found suspicious circumstances surrounding their execution.
The findings that other properties were unavailable for division because of separate assignment documents had become final and were not in dispute.
The Supreme Court found no reason to depart from the concurrent appellate findings on the will and gift deed.
issues.conclusion: The Court declined to interfere with the concurrent findings and dismissed the appeal.
issues.legal_principle: The Court stated that concurrent findings of fact should not normally be interfered with in the exercise of its power under Article 136 of the Constitution of India, and found no reason to interfere in this case.

predicates.supreme_court_discretionary_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal to the Supreme Court invoking its discretionary appellate power.
predicates.concurrent_appellate_factual_findings: The appellate court and the High Court have reached the same factual findings on the issue under appeal.
predicates.no_basis_for_interference: The Supreme Court finds no reason to depart from those concurrent factual findings.

issues.definition: In a discretionary Supreme Court appeal, concurrent appellate factual findings remain undisturbed when the Court finds no basis for interference.
